Who’s Suing Matters: Legal Representation and the Structure of Debt Collection in Virginia (2014–2024)

Team Challengers: Final Project

Addison Parman, Brett Navarro, Jonah Wilentz

April 2026

I. Introduction & Research Question

Research question: In Virginia’s warrant-in-debt cases, how much of the change in legal representation between 2014 and 2024 reflects real improvements in defendants’ access to counsel, and how much is driven by shifts in who is suing, where they file, and which communities bear the highest burden?

Our argument: The legal representation gap in Virginia debt collection is deep, persistent, and structurally rooted in the types of plaintiffs who dominate the system. Debt buyers and institutional creditors (who almost always bring attorneys) file overwhelmingly in lower-income communities, where defendants almost never have counsel. Apparent trends in statewide representation rates are largely compositional: they reflect changes in the mix of plaintiffs and the geography of filings, not meaningful progress in access to justice. Understanding who is suing, and where, is essential to evaluating whether the system is becoming fairer.

Debt collection lawsuits are the single most common civil case type in Virginia and many other states. Millions of low-income Americans are sued each year, most without a lawyer. This analysis uses Virginia General District Court records from virginiacourtdata.org (the Online Case Information System) to trace how representation patterns shifted between 2014 and 2024, and to show that the identity of the plaintiff and the economic profile of the community are central to understanding the representation gap.

II. Data & Methods

Variable construction

Legal representation (corrected)

Previously, we treated NA as the only indicator of no legal representation. But the attorney fields contain other values that also mean no attorney is present — things like SELF-REPRESENTED, SELF, PRO SE, NON, and NULL. Following the approach from the week 4 class example, we use str_detect() to catch these patterns before building the legal_rep variable.

This correction is itself a methodological finding: naive approaches to measuring representation in court data produce misleading results. Before correction, defendant representation appeared higher than what legal aid practitioners report, because self-represented litigants were being counted as having counsel.

Date variables

Plaintiff classification

A key part of our analysis is understanding who is filing these cases. Rickard (2020) documents that debt collection lawsuits have become the single most common civil case type in many states (Virginia included) and that this transformation has fundamentally changed how state courts operate. Pew’s review of studies from 2010 to 2019 found that fewer than 10% of debt collection defendants had a lawyer, compared to nearly all plaintiffs, and that over 70% of cases nationally ended in default judgment. Pew identifies a mechanism: lawsuits filed by debt buyers (mostly companies the defendant has never heard of) are less likely to receive a response at all. The composition of who is suing shapes not just representation rates but whether defendants even engage with the process.

We used str_detect() and str_to_lower() from stringr to search for keywords in plaintiff names and sort them into categories.

Demographic context (Census data)

We use tidycensus to pull county-level demographic characteristics from the ACS 5-year estimates (2022). The 5-year ACS is necessary for Virginia localities (many are too small for the 1-year ACS), and a single cross-section serves as a solid midpoint for relatively slow-changing demographics.

Median household income is a particularly important variable for this analysis. It serves as our primary measure of a community’s economic position, and it connects our two main threads: we use it to show both where different plaintiff types concentrate their filings and how defendant representation varies across the income spectrum. A locality with a median household income of $40,000 faces a fundamentally different legal landscape than one at $100,000 — not because the law is different, but because the residents’ ability to retain counsel, take time off work for court appearances, and navigate the legal system is largely shaped by economic resources.

III. Key Findings

A. The Representation Asymmetry

The structural imbalance in legal representation is the defining feature of Virginia’s debt collection system and it has not meaningfully changed between 2014 and 2024. Total filings declined from approximately 281,000 in 2014 to roughly 240,000 in 2024, though Sleight (2025) reports that 2024 represented a 27% surge over 2023 levels, meaning our second snapshot reflects a system in rebound.

The Legal Services Corporation’s Justice Gap report (2022) estimates that low-income Americans do not receive adequate legal help for approximately 92% of their substantial civil legal problems. The LSC/ODGA (2025) report, which analyzed Virginia debt collection filings from 2018 to 2023 (the period between our two snapshots), found that consumer representation reached approximately 1.9% by 2023, while debt collector representation rose to about 81%. Our data confirm this picture on both ends of the timeline.

The gap between plaintiff and defendant representation dwarfs any year-over-year movement. Even a doubling of defendant representation would still leave the vast majority of defendants without counsel.

B. Who Is Suing Matters

This is the core finding of our project As Rickard (2020) documents, the rise of debt buyers as plaintiffs has reshaped state civil courts nationally. Our data show that the type of plaintiff is strongly associated with both representation rates and the communities where cases are filed, making plaintiff composition a key driver of the patterns we see here.

Representation by plaintiff type

The representation asymmetry is not uniform, it varies dramatically by who is doing the suing. This is consistent with what LSC/ODGA (2025) found: 79% of debt collectors had legal representation compared to just 2% of consumers, and in contested cases, represented consumers won favorable judgments at 11 times the rate of unrepresented consumers.

The plaintiff types with the widest representation gaps (debt buyers, banks, and medical providers) are the institutional plaintiffs that mostly dominate the system. This means the overall representation gap is not just a feature of the system, it is produced by the types of plaintiffs who file the most cases.

The UVA story

UVA’s aggressive medical debt collection practices received significant public scrutiny around 2019, leading to policy changes. Since we treat all UVA plaintiffs as likely medical debt cases (per Professor Claibourn’s guidance), we can check whether their filings differ between 2014 (before the policy change) and 2024 (after it). This is a concrete example of how plaintiff behavior (not just defendant resources) shapes the landscape.

## Total UVA cases: 19174

C. Who Is Suing Where: Plaintiff Types and Community Income

The “who’s suing matters” finding becomes even more consequential when we examine where different plaintiff types concentrate their filings. This is where median household income comes into play.

Median household income captures a community’s overall economic position in a way that directly relates to the legal representation question. In lower-income localities, residents are less likely to be able to afford an attorney, less likely to have flexible work schedules that allow them to appear in court, and less likely to have the financial literacy and legal knowledge to navigate the system on their own. If institutional plaintiffs — the ones with the widest representation gaps — disproportionately file in these communities, then the justice gap is not randomly distributed, but concentrated precisely where people are most vulnerable.

The chart below answers a critical question: are the plaintiff types with the largest representation gaps also the ones filing in the poorest communities? For each plaintiff type, we compute the case-weighted average median household income of the localities where they file. This tells us not just where a plaintiff type has any presence, but where the bulk of their cases land. If debt buyers and medical collectors (who carry representation gaps of 70+ percentage points) are concentrated in localities with the lowest median incomes, then the structural asymmetry of the system is not just large, but likely targeted.

This analysis closes the loop on our argument. The representation gap is produced by specific types of plaintiffs filing in specific types of communities. The plaintiff types with the widest representation gaps concentrate their filings in the localities with the lowest median incomes and highest poverty rates. The burden of the justice gap falls precisely where communities can least afford it.

D. The Double Burden: Filing Rates, Income, and Representation

The relationship between community income and the representation gap extends beyond plaintiff type. Lower-income localities face a compounding disadvantage: they are sued more often and represented less!

As median household income decreases, per-capita filing rates increase and defendant representation rates decrease. Combined with our finding that institutional plaintiffs — the ones with the widest representation gaps — concentrate their filings in these same communities, we can confirm the structure of debt collection litigation in Virginia systematically disadvantages the communities least equipped to respond.

Representation over time by community type

Splitting localities into income terciles lets us check whether the representation gap is narrowing in lower-income communities or remaining entrenched.

IV. Discussion & Interpretation

The representation gap in Virginia debt collection is deep, persistent, and structurally produced by the types of plaintiffs who dominate the system:

The gap is large and stable. Plaintiff representation rates hover near 80%; defendant representation remains in the low single digits.

Who is suing shapes the gap. Debt buyers and institutional creditors almost always bring attorneys; their defendants almost never have one. The representation gap varies dramatically by plaintiff type, meaning that shifts in the plaintiff landscape can mechanically move the statewide representation rate without any change in defendants’ actual access to counsel.

The burden falls on lower-income communities. Institutional plaintiffs file disproportionately in lower-income, higher-poverty localities, the same communities where defendant representation is lowest and per-capita filing rates are highest. The “who is suing” story and the “where they’re suing” story overlap: the plaintiffs with the widest representation gaps concentrate their filings where defendants are least likely to have counsel and where the economic consequences of an adverse judgment are most severe.

What we cannot yet say: We cannot determine whether defendant representation actually changes case outcomes, though LSC/ODGA (2025) found that represented consumers win at 11 times the rate of unrepresented ones. We cannot identify which specific legal aid programs are responsible for any within-locality gains. And we cannot rule out that changes in how attorney fields are recorded over time may create artificial trends.

V. Limitations & Next Steps

Limitations: This analysis relies on two primary snapshot years (2014 and 2024) with intervening years for context. The plaintiff classifier is keyword-based and leaves a substantial “Other/Unclassified” category. We use a single Census cross-section (2022 ACS 5-year) rather than year-matched demographic estimates. And the analysis is observational — we can document associations between plaintiff types, community characteristics, and representation, but cannot establish causal relationships.

Next steps: Outcome analysis — connecting representation to plaintiff win rates, default judgments, and fee imposition — would quantify the stakes of the representation gap. Legal aid funding data from nonprofit tax records could help explain within-locality variation. And spatial mapping of filing rates and representation across Virginia would make the geographic concentration of the burden visible.

VI. Conclusion

The story of legal representation in Virginia debt collection dominated by institutional plaintiffs who almost always bring attorneys, suing individual defendants who almost never have one. This asymmetry is produced by the types of creditors who file the most cases, and it falls hardest on the lowest-income communities in the state.

Apparent changes in statewide representation rates (whether up or down) cannot be read at face value. Our plaintiff classification and demographic analysis point to the same conclusion: compositional shifts in who is suing and where they file can create the appearance of changing access without any real change in whether defendants can get a lawyer.

If the goal is to close the representation gap, the data suggests that interventions need to be targeted where institutional plaintiffs file most heavily — in lower-income communities where defendants are least likely to have counsel and where the consequences of unrepresented litigation are most severe.
